analogy.p: Imagine a team making sandwiches that needs bread, filling and people to make them. If there is only one loaf, extra filling and extra people will not make any more sandwiches because **bread is the limiting factor**. Give the team more bread and output rises until another ingredient (such as filling or the number of people) runs short, so the output levels off. In the same way, photosynthesis needs light, CO₂ and a suitable temperature, and the scarcest one limits the rate. The analogy breaks down because temperature in a plant does not simply run out: too much heat actually destroys the enzymes, so the rate falls instead of just levelling off.

bullets: Learn the four factors: **temperature, light intensity, CO₂ concentration, amount of chlorophyll**.
Define **limiting factor**: the factor in shortest supply that stops the rate rising, even though other factors are plentiful.
Interpret graphs: rising section = that factor is limiting; plateau = another factor is now limiting.
Higher tier only: **light intensity ∝ 1/d²** (inverse square law) and calculations with it.
Describe and explain **Required Practical 6** (pondweed, distance of the lamp, counting bubbles or measuring gas volume).
Explain the **economics** of controlling conditions in greenhouses (cost of heaters, lamps, CO₂ versus extra crop).
Links to enzymes (temperature), leaf adaptations (CO₂ uptake) and food security.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.4.1.2 asks you to **explain the effects of four factors on the rate of photosynthesis**: **temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll**. You must understand that these can each be a **limiting factor**, interpret graphs of photosynthesis rate, and (Higher tier) use the **inverse square law** for light intensity. You must also describe **Required Practical 6** and explain the **economics of adding heat, light or carbon dioxide in greenhouses**. Examiners reward answers that name the limiting factor and then say **why** the rate stops rising, rather than only describing the graph.

bullets: Word equation: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**; light energy is absorbed by **chlorophyll** in the **chloroplasts**.
Symbol equation: **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂** (balanced: 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side).
**Rate = amount of product (or reactant) ÷ time**, e.g. **cm³ of oxygen per minute** or bubbles per minute.
Ways to measure rate: count **bubbles** of oxygen, collect and measure **volume of gas**, measure **CO₂ uptake**, or measure the **increase in biomass/starch**.
A higher rate means more glucose is produced each minute, which means more growth and more food for the plant.
The reaction is **endothermic** because it takes in energy (light) from the surroundings.
Oxygen is a **product**, so the more oxygen produced per minute, the faster the rate of photosynthesis (in a controlled experiment).
core.p: Photosynthesis is an **endothermic reaction** in which energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the chloroplasts. The word equation is **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen** (in the presence of light and chlorophyll) and the symbol equation is **6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂**. The **rate** of photosynthesis is how fast the reaction happens, which means how much glucose or oxygen is made, or how much carbon dioxide is used, in a given time. In school practicals we measure the rate indirectly using the **oxygen given off** because oxygen bubbles from pondweed are easy to see and count.

bullets: Limiting factor: a variable that, when it is in short supply, **stops the rate of photosynthesis from increasing**.
More than one factor can limit at different times, and **which one limits depends on the conditions** (night, winter, a sealed greenhouse).
Only the factor in shortest supply is limiting; the others are present in **excess**.
Increasing the **limiting** factor increases the rate; increasing a non-limiting factor has **no effect**.
At low light intensity, **light is limiting**; on a warm bright day, **CO₂ concentration** is often limiting.
In cold conditions, **temperature** is often limiting because the **enzymes** work slowly.
The idea is the same as a production line: the slowest stage sets the output.
core.p: A **limiting factor** is the factor that is in the **shortest supply** relative to what the plant could use, so it **limits the rate** of photosynthesis. Photosynthesis needs several things at once, so the slowest or scarcest one controls how fast the whole process can go. If you increase a limiting factor the rate rises, but if you increase a factor that is **not** limiting, nothing changes. Once the limiting factor has been increased enough, a different factor becomes limiting and the rate levels off.

bullets: At low light intensity the rate **increases in proportion** to the light intensity: a straight line through the origin.
The plateau shows light is **no longer limiting**; **CO₂ concentration or temperature** (or chlorophyll) must be limiting instead.
No light = **no photosynthesis** (but respiration still happens).
Light energy is absorbed by **chlorophyll** in the **chloroplasts**, so more light means more energy for the reaction.
Light intensity decreases with **distance** from a lamp (Higher tier: **inverse square law**).
Very high intensities can also heat the plant or lamp area, so in experiments use an **LED lamp** or a heat shield.
In the UK, light is often limiting in **winter** because days are short and the sun is low.
core.p: Light provides the **energy** for photosynthesis, and **chlorophyll absorbs** that light energy so it can be used to make glucose. As light intensity increases from zero, the rate rises steadily because more energy is available to drive the reaction, so at low light intensity **light is the limiting factor**. The rate is **directly proportional** to light intensity in this first part of the graph. At higher intensities the graph **levels off** because something else (CO₂ concentration or temperature) has become limiting, and extra light makes no difference.

bullets: Air contains about **0.04% CO₂**, so CO₂ is often in short supply.
The rate **rises** as CO₂ concentration rises, then **levels off** when another factor (light or temperature) becomes limiting.
CO₂ enters the leaf by **diffusion** through the **stomata**, so closed stomata (e.g. in drought) reduce the CO₂ supply.
In pondweed experiments, **sodium hydrogencarbonate** dissolved in the water supplies extra CO₂.
Greenhouse growers can **enrich the air with CO₂** (e.g. burning paraffin, which also gives heat).
If CO₂ is the limiting factor, adding more light or heat will **not** raise the rate.
Link: the CO₂ taken in is built into **glucose**, so a higher CO₂ supply means a higher **rate of glucose production** until something else limits.
core.p: Carbon dioxide is one of the **reactants**, so the plant needs a supply to make glucose. The air contains only about **0.04% carbon dioxide**, which is very low, so on a bright, warm day **CO₂ concentration is often the limiting factor**. Increasing the CO₂ concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis until another factor becomes limiting, when the graph plateaus. This is why greenhouse growers sometimes add extra carbon dioxide.

bullets: Low temperature: particles have **less kinetic energy**, so fewer successful collisions between enzymes and substrates and a **slow rate**.
As temperature rises, the rate **increases** because there are more frequent, more energetic collisions.
At the **optimum** the rate is at its maximum (the optimum varies between species).
Above about **45 °C** the **enzymes denature**: the **active site changes shape**, so the substrates no longer fit and the rate drops quickly.
Denaturation is **permanent**, so the rate does not recover if the temperature falls again.
The graph is **not symmetrical**: it rises gradually but falls steeply after the optimum.
Temperature is often limiting in **cold weather**, but is rarely the limiting factor in the UK in summer.
Plants also lose water faster when hot, which can make the **stomata close**, reducing CO₂ entry.
core.p: The reactions of photosynthesis are controlled by **enzymes**, so temperature affects the rate in the same way it affects any enzyme-controlled reaction. As temperature rises from a low value, the particles have more **kinetic energy**, collide more often with more energy, so the rate **increases**. At the **optimum temperature** the rate is at its highest. Above roughly **45 °C** the enzymes begin to **denature**: their active sites change shape so substrates no longer fit, and the rate **falls sharply**.

bullets: Chlorophyll **absorbs light** (mainly red and blue light), reflecting green, which is why leaves look green.
Less chlorophyll = **less light absorbed** = lower rate of photosynthesis.
Parts of leaves that **lack chlorophyll** (white parts of variegated leaves) cannot photosynthesise.
Causes of low chlorophyll include **plant diseases** (e.g. **tobacco mosaic virus** causes discolouration) and **magnesium ion deficiency** (magnesium is needed to make chlorophyll).
Yellowing leaves (**chlorosis**) are a sign that chlorophyll is lacking.
Chlorophyll is a **limiting factor** that is usually fixed, rather than changed minute to minute like light or CO₂.
Link: leaf cells at the top of the leaf (**palisade mesophyll**) have many chloroplasts to absorb as much light as possible.
core.p: **Chlorophyll** is the green pigment in chloroplasts that **absorbs light energy** for photosynthesis. The more chlorophyll a plant has, the more light it can absorb, so the rate of photosynthesis can be higher. If a plant has **less chlorophyll**, it absorbs less light and the rate of photosynthesis is lower even when light, CO₂ and temperature are ideal. The amount of chlorophyll can be reduced by **disease or mineral deficiency** and by natural variation, as in **variegated leaves**.

bullets: **Rising section**: the factor on the x-axis is the **limiting factor** because increasing it increases the rate.
**Plateau**: the factor on the x-axis is **no longer limiting**; **another factor** (name possible ones) is now limiting.
Do **not** say the reaction has "stopped" at a plateau; the rate is **constant**, not zero.
A **straight, steep** rise through the origin means the rate is **directly proportional** to the factor.
On a temperature graph, a **peak then fall** shows the **optimum**, followed by **enzyme denaturation**.
To compare rates from a curve, quote **values with units** from the axes (e.g. "at 40 units the rate is 12 cm³/min").
Higher tier maths: the rate at one point on a curve = the **gradient of a tangent** drawn at that point.
A graph where the rate **never plateaus** within the range tested means the factor is still limiting everywhere.
core.p: Graphs of the rate of photosynthesis against one factor all follow the same pattern, and examiners ask you to **describe** and **explain** them. In the first part of the graph the line rises: the factor on the x-axis is **limiting**. When the line **levels off** (plateau), that factor is **no longer limiting**, so a different factor must be limiting. To answer well, say what the graph shows, name the limiting factor in each section and give the reason using the science of the reaction.

bullets: Where the two curves **overlap** (low light), the factor that **differs between the curves is not limiting**; light is.
Where the curves **separate**, the factor that differs (e.g. CO₂ or temperature) **is limiting** on the lower curve.
The upper curve plateaus at a **higher rate** because more of the second factor was provided.
On the lower curve's plateau, the limiting factor is the one that was **kept lower** in that experiment.
The point where a curve **starts to level off** shows where light stops being limiting.
Compare the two plateau values using a **calculation**, e.g. "rate doubled from 6 to 12 cm³/min when CO₂ was increased".
The same logic works for any pair of factors shown on the graph.
core.h: Graphs with two factors on one set of axes
core.p: Exam questions often show **two or more curves** on one graph, such as rate against light intensity at two different temperatures or CO₂ levels. The curves help you find which factor is limiting at each point. The **plateau of the upper curve is higher** because the second factor has been increased. At very low light intensity the curves **overlap**, because light is limiting in both cases and the other factor makes no difference.

bullets: **I ∝ 1/d²**, or **I = k ÷ d²**, where k is a constant for the lamp.
Doubling d: new intensity = **(1/2)² = 1/4** of the original.
Trebling d: new intensity = **(1/3)² = 1/9** of the original.
Halving d: new intensity = **(2)² = 4 times** the original.
To compare two distances: **I₂ = I₁ × (d₁ ÷ d₂)²**.
A graph of intensity against distance is a **steeply falling curve**; a graph of intensity against 1/d² is a **straight line through the origin**.
Use **1/d²** as the x-axis (relative light intensity) to test whether rate is proportional to light intensity.
Assumes a point source in a dark room; stray light and reflections cause errors.
core.h: The inverse square law for light intensity (Higher tier only)
core.p: Light intensity from a lamp **decreases as you move away**, and not in a simple way. The **inverse square law** says that light intensity is **inversely proportional to the square of the distance** from the source: **light intensity ∝ 1/d²**. This means that if you **double** the distance, the intensity falls to **one quarter**, and if you **treble** the distance it falls to **one ninth**. In Required Practical 6 you often use 1/d² as a measure of relative light intensity.

bullets: **1.** Set up a beaker of water containing **sodium hydrogencarbonate** to supply CO₂ and place a piece of pondweed of **fixed length** in it, under an inverted funnel with an inverted test tube above (or attach a capillary tube/gas syringe).
**2.** Place a **lamp** at a measured distance from the beaker using a **metre ruler**; start with a short distance, e.g. 10 cm.
**3.** Turn off other lights (close blinds) so the only light is from the lamp.
**4.** Leave the plant for a few minutes to **acclimatise** until bubbles are produced steadily.
**5.** **Count the bubbles** released in a fixed time (e.g. 1 minute), or measure the **volume of gas** collected in a set time.
**6.** Repeat the count at the same distance at least 3 times and calculate a **mean**.
**7.** Move the lamp to a new distance (20, 30, 40, 50 cm) and repeat, allowing the plant to adjust each time.
**8.** Calculate the rate (bubbles per minute or cm³ per minute) and plot a graph of rate against distance, or rate against **1/d²**.
core.h: Required Practical 6: method (effect of light intensity on rate of photosynthesis)
core.p: The aim is to investigate how the **distance of a light source** (and so the light intensity) affects the rate of photosynthesis, using an aquatic plant such as **Cabomba or Elodea (pondweed)**. The plant is placed in water, the lamp is placed at a measured distance, and the oxygen released is counted or collected. The method must be written in a clear order and each step should have a purpose. The distance is varied (for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm) and the rate is found at each distance.

bullets: **Independent variable:** distance from the lamp to the plant (or 1/d² as relative intensity).
**Dependent variable:** rate of photosynthesis = bubbles per minute or cm³ of oxygen per minute.

**Control variables:** same pondweed (same length and species), **temperature** of the water, **CO₂ concentration** (same amount of sodium hydrogencarbonate), same lamp and bulb, volume of water, time counted.

**Controlling temperature:** use an **LED lamp** or place a **beaker of water as a heat shield** between lamp and plant, or use a water bath, because a hot lamp would raise the temperature and change the rate.
**Errors:** bubble size varies so counting is **subjective**; the stream of bubbles may be hard to count; light from windows alters the intensity; the plant takes time to adjust.
**Improvements:** collect gas in a **gas syringe or capillary tube** and measure the volume; **repeat and take means**; use a **dark room**; **measure distance from the plant** accurately.
**Safety:** keep **electrical equipment away from water**, take care with a **hot lamp** (burns), glassware may break.
**Expected result:** rate **decreases as distance increases** because light intensity falls (Higher: ∝ 1/d²); the graph may level off at close distances when another factor limits.
core.h: Required Practical 6: variables, errors and improving the experiment
core.p: You need to identify the variables and explain how each is controlled, and to evaluate the method. The **independent variable** is the distance of the lamp (so the light intensity), and the **dependent variable** is the rate of oxygen production. The **control variables** include temperature, CO₂ concentration, the plant and the lamp. Counting bubbles is simple but not very accurate, so collecting and measuring the gas volume is better.

bullets: **Rate = volume of oxygen ÷ time** (cm³ ÷ min = **cm³/min**).
**Mean** = sum of repeats ÷ number of repeats; ignore **anomalous** results.
**Percentage change** = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
**Compare rates** by dividing one by the other: "the rate was **2 times** greater".
**Plot graphs:** the independent variable (distance or intensity) on the x-axis, rate on the y-axis, with units on both axes.
**Higher tier:** draw a **tangent** to the curve at a point and calculate **change in y ÷ change in x** to find the rate at that point.
Use the **inverse square law** to convert distance to relative intensity: relative intensity = **1 ÷ d²**.
Check answers make sense: a rate must be positive and in the right units.
core.p: Several simple calculations appear in this topic, and showing your working earns marks even if the final answer is wrong. Rate is calculated by dividing the amount produced by the time taken. You should also be able to find a **mean** of repeats, work out a **percentage change**, read values from a graph and (Higher tier) find the **gradient of a tangent**. Always include the **correct units**, usually **cm³/min** or **bubbles/min**.

bullets: **Heat:** heaters keep the temperature at the optimum, especially at night and in winter; the cost of **fuel/electricity** must be weighed against faster growth.
**Light:** artificial lamps allow photosynthesis at night and in winter; this uses **electricity**, which costs money.
**CO₂:** extra CO₂ can be added by burning **paraffin**, which gives off both **heat and CO₂**, so it can raise two factors at once.
A greenhouse **retains heat** (glass traps heat) and protects plants from wind, pests and frost.
There is **no point adding more** of a factor once another becomes limiting, because the extra cost gives no extra yield.
**Profit** = income from the extra crop − extra cost of heating, lighting and CO₂.
Evaluation points: costs can be reduced by **using only the factor that is limiting** at the time; large crops may justify expensive control.
Too much heat can **denature enzymes** and too many lights can make the plants overheat, so the conditions must be **monitored**.
core.h: Greenhouses and the economics of controlling photosynthesis
core.p: Farmers who grow crops in greenhouses can **control** the limiting factors to increase the rate of photosynthesis, giving a larger crop, a **faster crop** and a higher **yield**. They can add **artificial light**, **heaters** to keep the temperature near the optimum, and **extra carbon dioxide**. Each of these costs money, so growers must decide if the **extra income** from the bigger crop is greater than the **extra cost**. The aim is to **keep the conditions near the optimum** while keeping costs low, which is a balance between **profit and cost**.

bullets: **Enzymes:** temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis because the reactions are controlled by enzymes (optimum temperature, denaturation).
**Diffusion and leaf structure:** CO₂ enters through **stomata** by diffusion; spongy mesophyll air spaces give a large surface area.
**Transpiration:** hot, dry or windy conditions increase water loss and may close stomata, reducing CO₂ uptake.
**Uses of glucose:** the glucose produced is used for respiration, starch, cellulose, protein and fats (next spec point).
**Food security:** controlling limiting factors increases crop yield for a growing population.
**Ecology/carbon cycle:** photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere.
**Practical skills:** variables, repeats, means, validity, risk assessment.
core.p: This topic draws on many other parts of the GCSE course, so the ideas link neatly into extended answers. Temperature links to **enzymes** and **denaturation**, CO₂ links to **diffusion through stomata**, and water loss links to **transpiration**. Rate of photosynthesis also underpins **food security** because higher rates give bigger crops, and it affects the **carbon cycle** and the **oxygen** and **carbon dioxide** levels in the atmosphere.

exam: **Define a limiting factor (1 mark):** "a factor that is in short supply and limits the rate of photosynthesis".
**Describe a graph (2-3 marks):** quote values with units, say where the rate rises, where it plateaus, and use comparative words ("as ... increases, the rate increases").
**Explain a plateau (2 marks):** the factor on the x-axis is no longer limiting AND another factor (name one) is limiting.
**Explain a rising section (2 marks):** the factor on the x-axis is limiting, so increasing it increases the rate.

**Temperature (3 marks):** rises with temperature (more kinetic energy / more collisions) then enzymes denature above about 45 °C, so the rate falls; denaturation changes the shape of the active site.
**Calculations (2-3 marks):** write the equation, substitute, and give the answer with units (cm³/min). For inverse square: I₂ = I₁ × (d₁ ÷ d₂)².

**Required practical (4-6 marks):** include lamp at measured distance, controlled temperature (heat shield/LED), same CO₂ (sodium hydrogencarbonate), counting bubbles or gas volume in a fixed time, repeats and mean.
**Variables:** independent = distance/light intensity; dependent = rate (bubbles or cm³ per min); control = temperature, CO₂, plant, lamp.

**Evaluate greenhouse economics (6 marks):** benefits (faster growth, higher yield, year-round), costs (fuel, electricity), balance (profit), and a conclusion with a reason (only add the limiting factor).
**Command words:** *Describe* = say what happens; *Explain* = give reasons using "because"; *Evaluate* = weigh both sides and conclude.
**Graph tips:** read the axes and units first; for two curves, identify where they overlap or separate and what that tells you.

mistakes.r: The rate is constant, not zero; another factor (name it, e.g. CO₂ or temperature) is now the limiting factor.
mistakes.w: The graph levels off because the reaction has stopped.

mistakes.r: Only if light is the limiting factor; once another factor limits, more light has no effect.
mistakes.w: Increasing the light always increases the rate.

mistakes.r: Enzymes are not alive; they denature, because the active site changes shape and the substrate no longer fits.
mistakes.w: At high temperatures the enzymes are killed.

mistakes.r: Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water and releases oxygen (respiration is the reverse).
mistakes.w: Plants use oxygen in photosynthesis and release carbon dioxide.

mistakes.r: Intensity falls to a quarter (inverse square law: I ∝ 1/d²).
mistakes.w: Doubling the distance halves the light intensity.

mistakes.r: It raises the water temperature (a control variable) so the rate changes for the wrong reason; use an LED lamp or a heat shield.
mistakes.w: A hot lamp does not matter in the pondweed practical.

mistakes.r: Distance is the independent variable; the rate of photosynthesis (bubbles or cm³ per minute) is the dependent variable.
mistakes.w: The lamp distance is the dependent variable.

mistakes.r: Only worth it if CO₂ is limiting and the extra yield is worth more than the cost; otherwise it is wasted money.
mistakes.w: Adding more CO₂ in a greenhouse is always worth it.

mistakes.r: Chlorophyll absorbs light; less chlorophyll means less light absorbed and a lower rate.
mistakes.w: Chlorophyll is not important for the rate.

summary: AQA 4.4.1.2: you must explain how temperature, light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and the amount of chlorophyll affect the rate of photosynthesis, interpret graphs of limiting factors, use the inverse square law (Higher tier) and carry out Required Practical 6 with pondweed. You must also explain the economics of adding heat, light or CO₂ in greenhouses. It matters because limiting-factor graphs and the pondweed practical are regularly tested with calculations and 6-mark explanations.

terms.d: How quickly glucose or oxygen is made (or carbon dioxide used) in a given time.
A variable that, because it is in short supply, limits the rate of a reaction such as photosynthesis.
The amount of light energy falling on a surface; a limiting factor at low values.
The amount of carbon dioxide available to the plant; about 0.04% of air.
The temperature at which the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction is greatest.
The active site of an enzyme changes shape so that the substrate no longer fits; occurs at high temperatures (above about 45 °C).
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source: I ∝ 1/d² (Higher tier).
When one quantity increases, the other decreases by the same factor.
An aquatic plant such as Elodea or Cabomba used to measure the rate of photosynthesis by counting oxygen bubbles.
A chemical dissolved in the water in the pondweed practical to supply carbon dioxide.
The variable that you change in an investigation (e.g. distance of the lamp).
The variable that you measure (e.g. volume of oxygen per minute).
A variable that is kept the same so that it does not affect the results.
Pores (mainly in the lower leaf surface) through which carbon dioxide enters and water vapour leaves.
A reaction that transfers energy from the surroundings; photosynthesis takes in light energy.
The flat part of a graph where the rate stops increasing because another factor is limiting.
The mass or amount of crop produced.

worked.ans: 0.30 cm³/min at 10 cm and 0.15 cm³/min at 30 cm; the rate is 2 times greater at 10 cm.
worked.q: A student places pondweed at different distances from a lamp. At 10 cm, 2.4 cm³ of oxygen was collected in 8 minutes. At 30 cm, 0.9 cm³ was collected in 6 minutes. Calculate the rate of photosynthesis at each distance and say how many times greater the rate is at 10 cm. (4 marks)

worked.ans: 200 units at 30 cm and about 89 units at 45 cm.
worked.q: A lamp gives a light intensity of 800 units at a distance of 15 cm. Use the inverse square law to calculate the light intensity at 30 cm and at 45 cm. (3 marks, Higher tier)
steps: Check: distance doubled gives a quarter (800 ÷ 4 = 200); distance trebled gives a ninth.

worked.ans: Model answer: At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor, so as the light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis increases. The graph levels off because light is no longer limiting; another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature, is now in short supply. The farmer could raise the rate by increasing the carbon dioxide concentration or the temperature in the greenhouse, because increasing the light would have no effect.
worked.q: The graph shows the rate of photosynthesis rising with light intensity and then levelling off. Explain the shape of the graph. Explain how a farmer could increase the rate at the level part. (4 marks)
steps: Rising part: light intensity is the limiting factor, so increasing it increases the rate.
Level part: light is no longer limiting; another factor is in short supply.
Possible limiting factors: carbon dioxide concentration or temperature.
Farmer: increase the limiting factor (add CO₂ or heat), because adding more light will not help.
